setInfo: CoroCoro Comic #223 glossy promo (unnumbered), Japan
description: The genuine first Pokémon card ever released to the public. On October 15, 1996, the November issue of CoroCoro Comic — a Japanese monthly manga magazine from Shogakukan — hit newsstands with a two-card glossy insert of Pikachu and Jigglypuff. It landed five days before the Pokémon Trading Card Game officially went on sale. The cards were glued onto a sheet bound inside the magazine and had to be physically peeled out, which is why genuinely undamaged copies barely exist.
funFacts: Predates the official Pokémon TCG launch by five days — manga readers had it before the game was on shelves
The card credits Ken Sugimori as illustrator, but the real artist was Keiji Kinebuchi — an error on the very first Pokémon card ever printed
Because the cards were glued into the magazine, decades of damage means not a single PSA 10 is known to exist
estimatedValue: Enormous but volatile — sealed CoroCoro #223 issues have been valued near $150,000, while peeled singles vary wildly with condition

setInfo: Topps TMNT Series 1, 88 cards + 11 stickers
description: The first ever Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles trading card set, released by Topps to ride the wave of the franchise's animated series and first feature film. It kicked off a run of TMNT card sets that continued into the 1990s.
funFacts: Arrived at the peak of "Turtlemania," riding the first animated series and feature film
One of the earliest properties to successfully cross from Saturday-morning cartoon to trading card aisle
Set the template Topps would reuse for countless licensed-cartoon card sets through the '90s
estimatedValue: $5 – $50 for common cards, more for high-grade or rare inserts

setInfo: Bandai 1st Generation, Japan, #9
description: Most fans assume Konami's 1999 Official Card Game (Vol.1) was the first Yu-Gi-Oh! trading card, but Bandai actually released cards a year earlier, starting April 4, 1998, to tie into Toei's original anime. Blue-Eyes White Dragon appeared as card #9 in that very first Bandai generation — making this, not Vol.1, the true first Yu-Gi-Oh! trading card. Konami only took over the license in early 1999 after Bandai's final set.
funFacts: Predates the Yu-Gi-Oh! OCG that most fans think of as "the first" set by almost a year
Used a simpler dice-and-life-points system, not the card-battle rules Konami introduced in 1999
Bandai's cards are notoriously hard to find in top grades, making high-grade copies genuinely rare
estimatedValue: $20 – $300, more for high-grade examples — these thin, glossy cards are notoriously hard to find in top condition

setInfo: Topps Nintendo Game Pack (with an earlier 1982 Topps Donkey Kong "Jumpman" card predating the Mario name)
description: Mario's trading card history is a bit tangled: his earliest card appearance is arguably the 1982 Topps Donkey Kong set, where he appears as "Jumpman" before the Mario name existed. The first card set to use the Mario/Nintendo branding directly was the 1989 Topps Nintendo Game Pack. A proper full "Super Mario Bros." set from Topps in the US never actually happened.
funFacts: His actual first card appearance predates the "Mario" name itself
Nintendo's mascot never got a proper dedicated Super Mario Bros. set from Topps in the US — a genuine gap in the hobby
A great example of how "the first card" can be a legitimately disputed title
estimatedValue: $5 – $40 depending on card and condition

setInfo: Upper Deck Entertainment SpongeBob SquarePants Trading Card Game, Base Set
description: The first SpongeBob SquarePants trading card set, published by Upper Deck Entertainment on May 27, 2003 as a collectible card game tied to the show, four years after it first aired.
funFacts: Arrived four years after the show's debut, once its popularity was undeniable
One of the first major 2000s cartoons to get a full collectible card GAME, not just a sticker set
Rode the early-2000s CCG boom that followed in the wake of Pokémon and Yu-Gi-Oh!
estimatedValue: $5 – $30, more for first-edition or holo variants

setInfo: Gum, Inc. Mickey Mouse Set (R89/R90), 120 cards
description: Long before modern licensed card sets, Philadelphia's Gum, Inc. produced the first widely-distributed Mickey Mouse trading cards in 1935. Card fronts featured colorful comic-style artwork of Mickey and friends, while the backs carried jokes and trivia questions — one of the earliest examples of Disney characters hitting the collectible card market.
funFacts: Among the very first licensed non-sports trading cards of any Disney character, decades before modern sets
The 120-card set paired jokes and trivia on the back — an early example of "edutainment" card design
A cornerstone of the vintage non-sports card hobby; well-preserved examples are genuinely rare
estimatedValue: $20 – $500+ depending on card and grade; rare high-grade examples can go much higher

setInfo: Walt Disney's Winnie the Pooh 'Card Library' — Pooh Rummy / Concentration / Honey Tree (1965)
description: Pooh is one of the hardest 'first cards' to pin down. Despite being the third highest-grossing franchise on earth, he never got a classic gum-card debut. The earliest widely-collected Pooh card product is this 1965 Walt Disney 'Card Library' boxed set — three card games in one 39-cent pack — rather than a true collectible trading set. Dedicated Pooh trading cards only really arrive decades later.
funFacts: One of the biggest franchises in history with no clean 'rookie card' — a genuine gap in the hobby
The 1965 Pepys release is a card game in the Happy Families tradition, not a collectible trading set
A. A. Milne created Pooh in 1926; Disney only licensed him in 1961, which is why no pre-war card exists
estimatedValue: $30 – $200 for a complete boxed 1965 set, depending on condition

setInfo: Topps Star Wars Series 1 (Blue Border), #1 of 66
description: Released in June 1977, weeks after A New Hope hit cinemas, Topps' blue-bordered Series 1 was the first Star Wars trading card set ever made. Card #1 is a profile portrait of Luke Skywalker, and it sits at the head of the checklist as the franchise's undisputed rookie card. Packs held seven cards and one sticker, with card backs carrying story summaries and multi-card puzzles.
funFacts: A PSA-graded Luke Skywalker #1 has sold for $268,400, one of the highest prices ever paid for a non-sports card
Topps rushed the set out mid-release because nobody predicted how big the film would be
The blue border is the tell — Topps ran five colour-coded series for the first film alone
estimatedValue: $20 – $2,400 for a PSA 8; six figures for top-pop examples of card #1

setInfo: No first card — a marketing umbrella, not a character
description: Disney Princess is not a story or a character; it is a licensing banner Andy Mooney created in 2000 to sell Snow White, Cinderella, Ariel, Belle and others as one product line. Because it was assembled from characters who already existed, there is no single debut card for the brand itself.
funFacts: Snow White predates the Disney Princess brand by 63 years — her own card history starts far earlier
Mooney reportedly came up with the idea after seeing girls at a Disney On Ice show dressed in homemade princess costumes
Any "first Disney Princess card" would really be a first card for one of the individual princesses
estimatedValue: Not applicable — individual princess cards are collected instead
noCardReason: Disney Princess is a marketing brand launched in 2000 that bundles pre-existing characters together, so it has no debut trading card of its own. The individual princesses each have their own, much earlier, card histories.

setInfo: No documented collectible trading card release
description: Anpanman is one of the highest-grossing franchises ever made, but almost all of that revenue comes from toys, food licensing and home video aimed at Japanese pre-schoolers. Unlike Pokémon or Dragon Ball, it never got a Carddass, Amada or menko-style collector set that the trading card hobby recognises or tracks.
funFacts: Earns tens of billions of dollars almost entirely from toddler merchandise, not collectibles
Japanese card makers like Bandai and Amada built collector sets around shonen anime, not pre-school shows
A rare case of enormous commercial success with essentially zero presence in the card hobby
estimatedValue: Not applicable — no collectible card market exists
noCardReason: Anpanman is aimed at Japanese pre-schoolers and its merchandising went into toys and food rather than collectibles, so no trading card set tracked by the hobby was ever released.

setInfo: Mattel Barbie Series 1 / Deluxe First Edition Portfolio (No. 5533), 300 cards
description: Barbie had been on shelves for three decades before she got trading cards. Mattel's 1990 Series 1 set ran to 300 cards documenting Barbie's outfits and eras, and was also sold as a Deluxe First Edition portfolio in a vinyl binder containing all 300 plus 20 cards exclusive to that package.
funFacts: Arrived 31 years after the doll launched in 1959 — an unusually long wait for a first card
The cards function as a fashion archive, cataloguing outfits year by year rather than telling a story
The 20 portfolio-exclusive cards are the chase pieces for set collectors
estimatedValue: $25 – $120 for a complete sealed Deluxe First Edition portfolio

setInfo: No first card — the characters long predate the film series
description: The MCU began with Iron Man in 2008, and plenty of film-tie-in card sets followed from Upper Deck and others. But the MCU is a film continuity rather than a character, and every hero in it already had decades of card history through Marvel's comics. Asking for the MCU's rookie card really means asking for Iron Man's, or Spider-Man's.
funFacts: Iron Man, Captain America and Thor all had trading cards decades before the MCU existed
Marvel character cards go back to the 1960s, nearly 50 years before the first MCU film
Film-tie-in sets are collected as movie memorabilia rather than character debuts
estimatedValue: Not applicable — individual Marvel character cards are collected instead
noCardReason: The MCU is a film continuity launched in 2008, not a character, and every hero in it already had decades of comic-era trading cards. There is no meaningful "first MCU card".

setInfo: Wizards of the Coast Harry Potter TCG Base Set, #8/116 (Holo)
description: Wizards of the Coast — the publisher of Magic: The Gathering — launched the Harry Potter Trading Card Game in August 2001, three months ahead of the first film. The 116-card Base Set drew entirely on Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone. It became the second best-selling toy in the United States before Wizards abruptly stopped printing it after the 2003 expansion.
funFacts: Launched before the first film, so the artwork is book-based rather than film-based
Briefly the second best-selling toy in the entire US market
Wizards killed the game in 2003 and never publicly explained why
estimatedValue: $2 – $60 per card; holographic Harry Potter and Quidditch cards command the most

setInfo: Sanrio Collector's Card Plus (line launched 9 August 2023)
description: Hello Kitty launched in 1974 and has appeared on virtually every product imaginable, but a properly collectible trading card line took nearly 50 years to arrive. Sanrio's Collectors Card Plus, released on 9 August 2023, is the first structured, hobby-recognised Sanrio card set. Earlier Hello Kitty cards existed as stationery and sticker-card novelties rather than as a graded, collected series.
funFacts: A near 50-year gap between the character launching and getting a real collector card set
Sanrio built its empire on stationery and plush, which is why cards came so late
Hello Kitty's earlier 'cards' were sold as stationery novelties, not sealed collectible packs
estimatedValue: $1 – $40 per card; chase and secret rares run higher

setInfo: Upper Deck Call of Duty League, first full trading card release
description: Call of Duty has been one of the biggest entertainment franchises since 2003, but it took until 2021 to get real trading cards. Upper Deck's Call of Duty League set — alongside a Mountain Dew Game Fuel promotional release the same year — put professional esports players rather than in-game characters on cardboard, covering the Modern Warfare 2019 and Cold War seasons.
funFacts: The cards feature real esports pros, not the game characters — unusual for a video game franchise
An 18-year wait between the first game and the first official card set
Part of a broader push to make competitive gaming collectable like traditional sport
estimatedValue: $1 – $50 per card; autographed pro cards fetch more

setInfo: Topps Batman "Black Bat" #1
description: Topps rushed out several Batman sets in 1966 to ride the Adam West television series, and the Black Bat #1 is recognised as the first mainstream trading card of the character. The artwork across the 1966 Batman releases was painted by Norman Saunders, the illustrator behind Mars Attacks, giving the cards their lurid pulp-comic look.
funFacts: A Black Bat #1 has sold at auction for $45,000
Painted by Norman Saunders, the same artist behind the notorious Mars Attacks set
Topps ran Black Bat, Blue Bat and Red Bat variants in the same year, which still confuses collectors
estimatedValue: $50 – $45,000 depending on grade; the #1 card carries a huge premium

setInfo: Donruss Marvel Super Heroes #34 (of 66)
description: The 1966 Donruss Marvel Super Heroes set was the first Marvel trading card release of any kind, and card #34 is Spider-Man's debut on cardboard — just four years after he first appeared in Amazing Fantasy #15. The 66-card set is split into six 11-card character runs, with Spider-Man occupying #34 through #44, each showing a bright comic-panel illustration inside a white border.
funFacts: The first Marvel trading card set ever made, so it doubles as the debut card for Captain America, Thor and the rest
PSA receives more submissions from the Spider-Man run than any other section of the set
Arrived only four years after Spider-Man was created, making it an unusually early character debut
estimatedValue: $100 – $3,000+ depending on grade; high-grade #34 examples are scarce

setInfo: Hasbro / Milton Bradley Transformers Action Cards, 192 cards
description: Milton Bradley published the first Transformers trading cards in 1985, a 192-card run covering Autobot and Decepticon profiles plus scenes from the Generation 1 cartoon. They were sold in eight-card hanger packs rather than wax packs, and every pack included one of 24 mini stickers carrying a character's motto.
funFacts: Printed on playing-card stock with rounded corners, so they feel nothing like a normal trading card
Sold in oversized hanger packs designed to hang on retail pegs beside the toys
Series 1 was the only series ever produced in the US — all 192 cards came out at once
estimatedValue: $1 – $30 per card; sealed 1985 packs command a strong premium

setInfo: Bandai Naruto: The Path to Hokage (Japan), card 忍-1 / Ninja-1, 127 cards
description: Like Yu-Gi-Oh!, Naruto's real first card is Japanese and predates the version Western fans know. Bandai launched Naruto: The Path to Hokage in Japan in 2002, a 127-card set built from Ninja, Jutsu and Mission cards. Uzumaki Naruto is card 忍-1 — literally Ninja-1, the first card of the first set. The English-language Naruto CCG only followed in 2006 and ran until 2013.
funFacts: Card 忍-1 means Ninja-1 — it is literally the first card of the first Naruto set
Predates the English-language Naruto CCG that most Western fans think of as the original by four years
The card is printed with BANDAI 2002 MADE IN JAPAN along the bottom edge, dating it beyond doubt
estimatedValue: $1 – $80 per card; early rare foils are the chase pieces

setInfo: No trading card release
description: Dungeon Fighter Online is one of the highest-grossing games ever made, earning tens of billions almost entirely from in-game microtransactions in China and South Korea. It has essentially no Western merchandising footprint, and no physical trading card line has ever been produced for it.
funFacts: Out-earns most household-name franchises while being nearly unknown in the West
Revenue comes from in-game purchases rather than any physical merchandise
A clear example of how modern free-to-play economics can bypass collectibles entirely
estimatedValue: Not applicable — no trading cards exist
noCardReason: Dungeon Fighter Online earns its money through in-game microtransactions in Asian markets and has almost no physical merchandising, so no trading card set was ever made.

setInfo: Topps Chrome Disney #50 (shown: Orange Wave parallel, 21/25)
description: Cars is the franchise with no rookie card. When the film landed in 2006, Disney funnelled the merchandising into die-cast vehicles — one of the best-selling toy lines ever made — and never commissioned a debut trading card set the way Toy Story and The Lion King got from SkyBox. Lightning McQueen only properly reached cardboard with Topps Chrome Disney, roughly two decades late. Card #50 is his, and it runs all the way up to a one-of-one Superfractor.
funFacts: A top-20 global franchise that went nearly twenty years without a proper trading card set
Disney put the collectible money into die-cast vehicles instead — billions of dollars of little metal cars
The Topps Chrome #50 McQueen tops out at a Superfractor numbered 1/1, the only one in existence
estimatedValue: $5 for a base card up to five figures for the 1/1 Superfractor

setInfo: No trading card release
description: Candy Crush Saga has generated around twenty billion dollars, but it is a mobile puzzle game with no characters, no narrative and no collectible culture. King has licensed it into board games and slot machines, never into trading cards.
funFacts: Among the highest-grossing franchises on earth with essentially no characters to put on a card
Its entire revenue comes from in-app purchases rather than merchandise
Shows how the modern mobile era broke the old link between popularity and collectibles
estimatedValue: Not applicable — no trading cards exist
noCardReason: Candy Crush is a mobile puzzle game with no characters or story to build a card set around, so no trading cards were ever released.

setInfo: Upper Deck Comic Ball 1 — the first major Looney Tunes set
description: Looney Tunes cards are genuinely hard to date. Scattered Bugs Bunny cards turn up as far back as the 1960s, but they were regional novelties that the hobby never properly catalogued. The first major, widely-collected Looney Tunes release is Upper Deck's Comic Ball in 1990, which paired the characters with real baseball players — most famously Bugs Bunny alongside Nolan Ryan.
funFacts: Bugs Bunny cards exist from the 1960s, but they are so poorly documented that no one agrees which came first
Comic Ball is a genuine crossover — real MLB players sharing cards with cartoon characters
Upper Deck ran several Comic Ball series through the early 1990s off the back of its success
estimatedValue: $1 – $40 per card; Bugs Bunny and Nolan Ryan cards carry the premium

setInfo: SkyBox Toy Story, 90-card base set
description: SkyBox produced the first Toy Story cards in 1995 for the release of the first fully computer-animated feature film. Just over half the 90-card base set retells the story, with the rest given over to puzzle cards, pop-ups, and a final run of sixteen cards that assemble into models of four lead characters, four cards per character.
funFacts: Documents the first ever fully computer-animated feature film as it happened
Sixteen cards in the set are body parts that build into four character models
Designed for kids to cut up and play with, so undamaged sets are harder to find than they should be
estimatedValue: $15 – $60 for a complete 90-card base set

setInfo: SkyBox The Lion King Series 1, 90 cards
description: SkyBox's 1994 Lion King set was one of the biggest movie card releases of the decade. Series 1 runs to 90 cards retelling the film and covering the main characters, followed by an 80-card Series 2. Beyond card shops, the cards were handed out in Burger King Kids Meals, putting them in front of a huge audience.
funFacts: Distributed through Burger King Kids Meals as well as hobby shops
Series 1 and 2 together run to 170 cards — an unusually deep set for a single film
Lenticular and other interactive inserts made it one of the flashiest movie sets of the 1990s
estimatedValue: $15 – $50 for a complete Series 1 set; inserts are worth more

setInfo: Card games only — no collectible trading card set
description: Dora the Explorer is a top-25 franchise worldwide, but Nickelodeon put its licensing into toys, DVDs and pre-school games. The Dora card products that exist are playable card games — Go Fish, Crazy Eights, Kidz Cards tins from around 2006 — rather than a collectible set with a checklist to chase.
funFacts: The Dora cards that exist are Go Fish and Crazy Eights decks, not collectibles
Pre-school franchises rarely get collectible sets because the audience is too young to chase a checklist
Follows the same pattern as Anpanman: huge revenue, no hobby presence
estimatedValue: Not applicable — no collectible card market exists
noCardReason: Nickelodeon only ever released playable Dora card games such as Go Fish and Crazy Eights, never a collectible trading card set with a checklist.

setInfo: Fleer Pac-Man Stickers & Rub-Offs, 54 cards
description: Fleer put Pac-Man on cardboard in 1980, the same year the arcade cabinet arrived, making it one of the earliest video game trading card sets ever produced. The 54-card run pairs stickers with scratch-off rub-off game cards, and packs shipped with three stickers, three rub-offs and a stick of gum. Fleer followed it with Ms. Pac-Man in 1981 and Super Pac-Man in 1982.
funFacts: One of the first trading card sets built around a video game rather than a film or TV show
Packs contained an actual playable element — scratch-off rub-off game cards
Fleer moved fast: cards were on shelves the same year the arcade machine launched
estimatedValue: $2 – $40 per card; sealed wax packs and complete sets fetch more

setInfo: Sticker albums only — no trading card set
description: Paw Patrol is one of the biggest pre-school properties on earth, but its card presence is entirely Panini sticker collections sold in supermarkets — Big Truck Pups, Search & Rescue and others. These are sticker albums to fill, not trading card sets with a checklist of numbered cards to chase and grade.
funFacts: Every Paw Patrol Panini release is a sticker collection, not a trading card set
Follows the same pattern as Dora and Anpanman: pre-school shows rarely get collector cards
The audience is too young to chase a checklist, so publishers stick to sticker albums
estimatedValue: Not applicable — no trading card market exists
noCardReason: Paw Patrol has only ever had Panini sticker albums sold through supermarkets, never a numbered trading card set with a checklist for collectors to chase.

setInfo: Peanuts trading cards, first collectible series (1991)
description: Peanuts ran in newspapers from 1950 and its characters appeared on all kinds of printed novelties, some carrying 1958 and 1965 copyright dates. But the first proper Peanuts trading cards the hobby tracks arrive in 1991, timed to the strip's 40th anniversary, followed by ProSport's Peanuts Classics series. Four decades is one of the longest waits for a first card of any major franchise.
funFacts: Peanuts waited four decades from its 1950 debut before getting a real trading card set
Earlier Peanuts card novelties exist with 1958 and 1965 copyright dates, but none were collectible sets
Cryptozoic revived Peanuts cards decades later for the strip’s 75th anniversary
estimatedValue: $10 – $40 for a complete 33-card set

setInfo: Donruss Marvel Super Heroes — no dedicated Avengers debut set
description: The Avengers have no debut card of their own. The team formed in 1963, and its members first reached cardboard in the 1966 Donruss Marvel Super Heroes set — the same 66-card run that gave Spider-Man his first card — where Captain America, Thor and the others appear as individual heroes. A trading card set built specifically around the Avengers as a team would not arrive for decades.
funFacts: Shares its debut set with Spider-Man: the same 1966 Donruss release covers both
The Avengers appear as separate heroes, never as a team, on their earliest cards
The MCU made the Avengers a household name 45 years after their first cards
estimatedValue: $50 – $1,500 depending on hero and grade

setInfo: Panini Disney Frozen: The Ice Kingdom sticker and card collection
description: Frozen became the highest-grossing animated film ever made, and Panini moved quickly with the Frozen: The Ice Kingdom collection in 2014. Like most modern Disney properties it arrived as a sticker-and-card album sold through supermarkets rather than as sealed hobby packs, with a 168-sticker album to complete.
funFacts: Panini followed up with further Frozen and Frozen II collections through 2019
Sold as a supermarket album rather than hobby wax, so complete albums are the collectible
A reminder that the biggest animated film of its era never got a classic sealed card set
estimatedValue: $20 – $70 for a complete filled album

setInfo: No trading card release
description: Space Invaders effectively created the video game industry as a mass phenomenon in 1978, and it sits inside the top 30 highest-grossing franchises of all time. Despite that, no trading card set was ever made for it. Taito has licensed modern novelty playing-card decks, but nothing that functions as a collectible set with a checklist.
funFacts: Fleer put Pac-Man on cards in 1980, but nobody ever did the same for Space Invaders
The only Space Invaders cards are modern novelty poker decks, not collectibles
Its abstract pixel aliens gave illustrators almost nothing to build a card set around
estimatedValue: Not applicable — no collectible trading cards exist
noCardReason: No collectible Space Invaders trading card set has ever been produced. The only Space Invaders cards are modern novelty playing-card decks, which have no checklist and no collector market.

setInfo: Upper Deck World of Warcraft TCG: Heroes of Azeroth, 361 cards
description: Upper Deck launched the World of Warcraft Trading Card Game on 25 October 2006 with Heroes of Azeroth, its first set. Its cleverest idea was the loot card: ultra-rare pulls carrying codes that unlocked real in-game items, like a hippogryph pet or a turtle mount, tying the cardboard directly to the world's biggest MMO. The game ran to 21 expansions before ending in 2013.
funFacts: Loot cards redeemed for real in-game mounts and pets, which sent their prices soaring
Ran to 21 booster expansions between 2006 and 2013
One of the first card games where a card had direct value inside a video game
estimatedValue: $1 – $60 for most cards; unredeemed loot cards go far higher

setInfo: Topps Despicable Me 3 Trading Card Game
description: The Minions became one of the most merchandised characters of the 2010s, but their first proper trading cards did not arrive until Topps produced a Despicable Me 3 Trading Card Game in 2017 — seven years after the first film. A full Minions collectible card game from Card Fun followed years later, in 2024.
funFacts: Seven years passed between the first film and the first Topps trading card set
The Minions out-merchandised the films themselves long before anyone printed a card
A dedicated Minions collectible card game only arrived in 2024, well over a decade in
estimatedValue: $1 – $15 per card; sealed 2017 packs carry a small premium

setInfo: Leaf Star Trek, 72 cards
description: Leaf produced the first Star Trek trading cards in 1967, a 72-card black-and-white set drawn from episode stills and on-set bloopers. It barely reached the public: Leaf only distributed in Ohio and Illinois, and the set was pulled almost immediately over a licensing dispute. That makes it one of the rarest and most sought-after television card sets in the hobby.
funFacts: Recalled shortly after release over a licensing problem, which is why so few survive
Only ever distributed across Ohio and Illinois — it never went national
The text on the backs was largely invented and often has nothing to do with the episode shown
estimatedValue: $50 – $500+ per card; complete 1967 sets are genuinely rare

setInfo: Bandai Dragon Ball Carddass Set 1 (November 1988), 42 cards
description: Bandai launched Dragon Ball Carddass in November 1988, and Set 1 runs to 42 cards — 36 regular plus 6 prism cards. They were never sold in shops as packs: you fed coins into a Carddass vending machine and it dispensed cards one at a time. The format was a Japanese phenomenon and became the template Bandai reused for countless anime properties.
funFacts: Dispensed from coin-operated vending machines rather than sold in packs
Japan-only, which is why Western collectors discovered them decades late
The six prism cards in Set 1 are the original Dragon Ball chase cards
estimatedValue: $10 – $500+ depending on card and condition; early prisms are the prize
